text: Enrollment in five evening courses at a community college, 2024 and 2025

stem: Which course had the greatest percent increase in enrollment from 2024 to 2025?
explanation: Percent increase = (2025 − 2024) ÷ 2024. Pottery rose by 18/60 = 30%, ahead of Accounting (30/120 = 25%), Spanish (19/95 = 20%) and Web Design (28/140 = 20%); Photography fell. Web Design is the trap: it had the largest increase in students (28), but on a much larger base.

stem: What was the total enrollment in the five courses in 2025?
explanation: Add the 2025 column: 150 + 72 + 114 + 168 + 78 = 582. The total 495 is the 2024 column, a common slip when reading the wrong year.

stem: By what percent did enrollment in Photography decrease from 2024 to 2025?
explanation: The decrease was 80 − 72 = 8 students, and the base is the earlier year: 8/80 = 0.10 = 10%. Dividing by the 2025 figure (8/72 ≈ 11.1%) uses the wrong base.

text: Bicycles sold by a bicycle shop in each quarter of 2025, by type

stem: In the third quarter (Q3), what was the ratio of mountain bikes sold to road bikes sold?
explanation: In Q3 the shop sold 180 mountain bikes and 260 road bikes. 180 : 260 simplifies (divide by 20) to 9 : 13. Choosing 13 to 9 reverses the order the question asks for.

stem: Approximately what percent of all bicycles the shop sold in 2025 were mountain bikes?
explanation: Mountain bikes: 90 + 120 + 180 + 110 = 500. Road bikes: 140 + 210 + 260 + 150 = 760, so all bicycles total 1,260. 500/1,260 ≈ 39.7%, about 40%. The trap 66% comes from dividing by the road-bike total (500/760) instead of the overall total.

stem: Indicate all quarters in which the number of road bikes sold was at least 1.5 times the number of mountain bikes sold.
explanation: Compare road ÷ mountain each quarter: Q1 140/90 ≈ 1.56, Q2 210/120 = 1.75, Q3 260/180 ≈ 1.44, Q4 150/110 ≈ 1.36. Only Q1 and Q2 reach 1.5. Q3 has the tallest road bar, but the mountain bar is tall too, so its ratio is lower.

text: Average monthly rainfall in City P and City Q, January to June

stem: In how many of the six months shown did City P receive more rainfall than City Q?
explanation: City P is above City Q in April (95 vs 60), May (120 vs 45) and June (85 vs 30): 3 months. In March the lines are close, but P's 70 mm is still below Q's 75 mm, so counting March gives the wrong answer of 4.

stem: By what percent did City P's average rainfall increase from January to April?
explanation: The increase is 95 − 40 = 55 mm on a January base of 40 mm: 55/40 = 1.375 = 137.5%. Reading the 55 mm rise as 55% ignores the base, and 237.5% is 95/40, the April value as a percent of January rather than the increase.

stem: What was City Q's total average rainfall, in millimeters, for the six months shown?
explanation: Add City Q's six values: 110 + 90 + 75 + 60 + 45 + 30 = 410 mm. Take care to read City Q's line, which falls steadily, rather than City P's.

text: Employees of Firm K at its four offices, by job category

stem: What percent of the employees at the Pune office work in Support?
explanation: Pune has 48 Support employees out of 150 in total: 48/150 = 0.32 = 32%. Choosing 48% treats the head count as a percent; that works only for an office of exactly 100 people, such as Lagos.

stem: For the four offices combined, how many more employees work in Engineering than in Support?
explanation: Engineering: 48 + 36 + 25 + 72 = 181. Support: 30 + 16 + 10 + 48 = 104. The difference is 181 − 104 = 77. The option 104 is the Support total itself, not the difference.

stem: Indicate all offices at which Sales employees make up more than 25% of the office's employees.
explanation: Divide Sales by Total: Lagos 22/100 = 22%, Lima 28/80 = 35%, Oslo 15/50 = 30%, Pune 30/150 = 20%. Only Lima and Oslo exceed 25%. Pune has the most Sales staff (30), but they are a small share of its large office.

text: How a household divides its monthly budget of 3,200 dollars

stem: How many dollars does the household budget for Food each month?
explanation: Food is 20% of 3,200 dollars: 0.20 × 3,200 = 640 dollars. The other options are the dollar amounts of other slices (Utilities 256, Transport 384, Savings 480, Housing 1,120).

stem: If the household raised its Savings to 20% of the same 3,200-dollar budget, by how many dollars per month would Savings increase?
explanation: Savings would rise from 15% to 20%, an increase of 5 percentage points: 0.05 × 3,200 = 160 dollars. Choosing 640 gives the new Savings amount, not the increase.

stem: What is the combined monthly amount, in dollars, budgeted for Transport and Other?
explanation: Transport and Other together are 12% + 10% = 22% of the budget: 0.22 × 3,200 = 704 dollars. Adding the percentages first saves a step and avoids rounding.

text: Annual visitors to a science museum, 2020-2025

stem: For which year was the percent increase in visitors over the previous year the greatest?
explanation: Visitors rose from 95,000 to 150,000 in 2022, an increase of 55/95 ≈ 58%. The 2023 bar shows the largest rise in number (60,000), but on a base of 150,000 that is only 40%. 2021 was a decrease.

stem: What was the average (arithmetic mean) number of visitors per year, in thousands, for the six years shown?
explanation: The six bars total 180 + 95 + 150 + 210 + 245 + 260 = 1,140 thousand, and 1,140 ÷ 6 = 190 thousand. Dividing by 5 (one fewer than the number of years) gives the trap answer 228.

stem: The number of visitors in 2025 was what percent of the number in 2020? Give your answer to the nearest whole percent.
explanation: Divide 2025 by 2020: 260/180 ≈ 1.444, or about 144%. The question asks for 2025 as a percent of 2020, not the percent increase (which would be about 44%).

text: Average price per kilogram of five fruits at a city market, March and September

stem: Which fruit's price per kilogram rose by the greatest percent from March to September?
explanation: Bananas rose from 1.20 to 1.80 dollars, an increase of 0.60/1.20 = 50%. Cherries rose by the most dollars (3.60), but from a base of 9.00 that is only 40%; Grapes rose 15%, and Mangoes and Apples fell.

stem: At September prices, how many dollars would 3 kilograms of mangoes and 2 kilograms of grapes cost?
explanation: Use the September column: 3 × 3.60 = 10.80 and 2 × 6.90 = 13.80, for a total of 24.60 dollars. Using the March prices gives 3 × 4.80 + 2 × 6.00 = 26.40.

stem: Indicate all fruits whose price per kilogram changed by at least 20 percent, up or down, from March to September.
explanation: Compute each change against the March price: Mangoes −1.20/4.80 = −25%, Apples −0.50/2.50 = −20%, Grapes +0.90/6.00 = +15%, Bananas +50%, Cherries +40%. Decreases count too, and Apples' 20% meets 'at least 20 percent' exactly; only Grapes falls short.

text: Company W's 2025 revenue of 80 million dollars by region, and its number of stores in each region

stem: What was Company W's 2025 revenue from Europe, in millions of dollars?
explanation: Europe's slice is 25% of 80 million dollars: 0.25 × 80 = 20 million. Choosing 25 reads the percent as if it were the dollar amount.

stem: What was the average revenue per store in Asia in 2025, in thousands of dollars?
explanation: Asia's revenue is 0.30 × 80 = 24 million dollars, shared by 40 stores: 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6 million = 600 thousand dollars per store. The option 1,250 is Europe's figure (20 million ÷ 16 stores), and 2,400 forgets to divide by the number of stores.

stem: Asia's stores made up what percent of all of Company W's stores? Give your answer to the nearest whole percent.
explanation: There are 32 + 16 + 40 + 8 = 96 stores, of which 40 are in Asia: 40/96 ≈ 41.7%, which rounds to 42%. Note that this is more than Asia's 30% share of revenue; the pie and the table measure different things.

text: Average daily passengers on two tram lines in a city, July to December

stem: In which month was the difference between the average daily passengers on Line 1 and on Line 2 the greatest?
explanation: Subtract month by month: July 12, August 5, September 9, October 16, November 8, December 11 (thousand). The gap is widest in October, when Line 2 dipped while Line 1 rose. December has the highest values on both lines, but not the largest gap.

stem: By approximately what percent did average daily passengers on Line 2 increase from July to December?
explanation: Line 2 rose from 30 to 44 thousand, an increase of 14 thousand. 14/30 ≈ 0.467, about 46.7%. Dividing by the December value instead (14/44 ≈ 32%) uses the wrong base, and 147% is 44/30 expressed as a percent.

stem: What was the average (arithmetic mean) of Line 1's six monthly values, in thousands of passengers? Give your answer to the nearest tenth.
explanation: Line 1's values total 42 + 38 + 45 + 50 + 48 + 55 = 278 thousand. Dividing by 6 gives 46.33..., which rounds to 46.3.

text: Preferred study location of 400 surveyed university students, by year of study

stem: What percent of the second-year students surveyed prefer to study at home?
explanation: There are 200 second-year students and 70 of them chose Home: 70/200 = 35%. The trap 17.5% divides by all 400 students, and 57.4% divides by the 122 students who chose Home.

stem: Among the students who prefer a café, what is the ratio of first-year students to second-year students?
explanation: The Café row shows 28 first-year and 40 second-year students. 28 : 40 simplifies (divide by 4) to 7 : 10. The option 7 to 17 compares first-year students with all 68 café students, and 10 to 7 reverses the order.

stem: Indicate all locations that were preferred by more first-year students than second-year students.
explanation: Compare the two columns row by row: Library 64 > 46 and Dorm room 56 > 44, but Home 52 < 70 and Café 28 < 40. So only Library and Dorm room qualify.

text: Electricity generated in Region T by source, 2015, 2020 and 2025

stem: What was the total electricity generated from the four sources in 2025, in gigawatt-hours?
explanation: Add the four 2025 bars: 640 + 420 + 480 + 460 = 2,000 gigawatt-hours. The options 1,350 and 1,600 are the totals for 2015 and 2020, so check that you are reading the 2025 series.

stem: In 2025, by how many gigawatt-hours did wind and solar generation combined exceed gas generation?
explanation: Wind and solar together produced 480 + 460 = 940 gigawatt-hours in 2025, and gas produced 640, so the excess is 940 − 640 = 300. The option 940 is the combined total, not the difference.

stem: What percent of the total electricity generated from the four sources in 2025 came from solar?
explanation: Solar produced 460 of the 2,000 gigawatt-hours generated in 2025: 460/2,000 = 0.23 = 23%. Using the 2020 solar bar (150) by mistake gives a much smaller share.

text: Trees planted by four volunteer groups in spring, summer and autumn of one year

stem: How many more trees did Treeline plant in spring than in summer and autumn combined?
explanation: Treeline planted 410 trees in spring and 130 + 160 = 290 in summer and autumn together, so the difference is 410 − 290 = 120. The option 290 is the summer-plus-autumn total itself, and 280 subtracts only the summer figure.

stem: Approximately what percent of all the trees planted by the four groups were planted in spring?
explanation: Spring plantings total 340 + 280 + 410 + 220 = 1,250, and all plantings total 1,250 + 700 + 850 = 2,800. 1,250/2,800 ≈ 44.6%. The option 25% is summer's share (700/2,800), so be sure to use the spring column.

stem: Indicate all groups that planted more than 25% of their own trees in summer.
explanation: Find each group's total and its summer share: Green Hands 160/740 ≈ 22%, Root & Branch 190/720 ≈ 26%, Treeline 130/700 ≈ 19%, Canopy Club 220/640 ≈ 34%. Root & Branch qualifies only narrowly, so it pays to compute rather than eyeball: 25% of 720 is 180, and 190 > 180.

text: How a research scientist divides a 50-hour work week

stem: How many hours per week does the scientist spend on teaching?
explanation: Teaching takes 18% of 50 hours: 0.18 × 50 = 9 hours. Choosing 18 reads the percent as a number of hours, which would be right only for a 100-hour week.

stem: How many more hours per week does the scientist spend on lab experiments than on writing and email combined?
explanation: Writing and email together are 22% + 10% = 32%, so lab experiments exceed them by 36% − 32% = 4 percentage points. 4% of 50 hours is 2 hours. Choosing 4 stops at the percentage-point difference without converting it to hours.

stem: If the scientist's work week grew to 60 hours with the same percent distribution, how many more hours per week would be spent on writing?
explanation: Writing stays at 22% of the week, and the week grows by 10 hours, so writing grows by 0.22 × 10 = 2.2 hours (from 11 to 13.2 hours).

text: Applications received and applicants accepted by a graduate program, 2021-2025

stem: In which year was the acceptance rate (applicants accepted ÷ applications received) the lowest?
explanation: The rates are 80/400 = 20%, 90/450 = 20%, 91/520 = 17.5%, 96/480 = 20% and 102/600 = 17%. The lowest is 2025, even though that year had the most acceptances; 2023 is close behind at 17.5%.

stem: The number of applicants accepted in 2025 was approximately what percent greater than the number accepted in 2021?
explanation: Acceptances rose from 80 to 102, an increase of 22. Relative to the 2021 base, 22/80 = 0.275 = 27.5%. Choosing 22% mistakes the increase in people for a percent, and 18% (about 22/122) uses neither year as the base.

stem: How many applicants to the program were not accepted in 2023?
explanation: In 2023 the program received 520 applications and accepted 91 applicants, so 520 − 91 = 429 were not accepted.

text: Distance, driving time and number of deliveries for five delivery routes on one day

stem: Which route had the greatest average speed, in kilometers per hour?
explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time in hours: A 36/1.2 = 30, B 48/(4/3) = 36, C 25/1 = 25, D 42/(7/6) = 36, E 60/1.5 = 40 km/h. Route E is fastest. Routes B and D tie at 36 km/h, so neither can be the single greatest.

stem: On which route was the average driving time per delivery the longest?
explanation: Divide time by deliveries: A 72/18 = 4, B 80/24 ≈ 3.3, C 60/10 = 6, D 70/14 = 5, E 90/30 = 3 minutes. Route C has the longest time per delivery. Route E has the most total driving time, but it also has the most deliveries, so its time per delivery is the shortest.

stem: Indicate all routes on which the average distance per delivery was at most 2 kilometers.
explanation: Distance ÷ deliveries: A 36/18 = 2, B 48/24 = 2, C 25/10 = 2.5, D 42/14 = 3, E 60/30 = 2 km. 'At most 2' includes exactly 2, so A, B and E all qualify; leaving them out because none is below 2 is the trap.

text: Population and land area of the five districts of a city

stem: Which district has the greatest population density (people per square kilometer)?
explanation: Density = population ÷ area: North 700, East 900, South 500, West 700 and Central 96,000/40 = 2,400 people per square kilometer. West has by far the largest population, but it is spread over the largest area; small Central is the most crowded.

stem: Approximately what percent of the city's total population lives in West?
explanation: The total population is 84,000 + 126,000 + 45,000 + 210,000 + 96,000 = 561,000. West's share is 210,000/561,000 ≈ 37.4%. A quick check: one-third of 561,000 is 187,000, and West has more than that, so 33% is too low.

stem: How many more people per square kilometer live in East than in North?
explanation: East's density is 126,000/140 = 900 and North's is 84,000/120 = 700 people per square kilometer, a difference of 200. Comparing the raw populations (42,000 more people in East) answers a different question.

text: Online orders received by a bakery each month, January to August

stem: Between which two consecutive months did the number of online orders increase the most?
explanation: Orders rose by 700 from June (1,900) to July (2,600), the steepest segment of the line. July to August rose by 400 and March to April also by 400. August has the highest point, but the question asks about the largest rise, not the highest value.

stem: What was the average (arithmetic mean) number of online orders per month for the eight months shown?
explanation: The eight values total 12 + 15 + 14 + 18 + 21 + 19 + 26 + 30 = 155 hundred = 15,500 orders. Dividing by 8 gives 1,937.5. The trap 15,500 is the total, and 2,214 divides by 7 instead of 8.

stem: Indicate all months in which the bakery received fewer online orders than in the previous month.
explanation: The line dips twice: from 1,500 in February to 1,400 in March, and from 2,100 in May to 1,900 in June. Every other month rises, so only March and June qualify.

text: Final grades of the students in three classes taking the same course

stem: What percent of the students in Class Z received a grade of B?
explanation: Class Z has 32 students, and 12 of them received a B: 12/32 = 0.375 = 37.5%. Choosing 40% divides by 30, the size of the other two classes, and 12% reads the count as a percent.

stem: For the three classes combined, how many students received a grade of C or better?
explanation: 'C or better' means A, B or C. Class X: 6 + 10 + 8 = 24; Class Y: 9 + 8 + 7 = 24; Class Z: 4 + 12 + 10 = 26. In all, 24 + 24 + 26 = 74. The option 88 also counts the D grades, and 92 is every student.

stem: Of all the students in the three classes who received an A, what percent were in Class Y? Give your answer to the nearest whole percent.
explanation: There were 6 + 9 + 4 = 19 A grades, and 9 of them were in Class Y: 9/19 ≈ 47.4%, which rounds to 47%. Dividing by Class Y's size (9/30 = 30%) answers a different question: what share of Class Y earned an A.

text: Tourists visiting Island R each month, January to June, and their average spending per visit

stem: In which month was the total spending by tourists (number of tourists × average spending per tourist) the lowest?
explanation: Multiply the two displays month by month: January 20,000 × 600 = 12.0 million dollars, February 14.0, March 16.5, April 20.0, May 24.0 and June 23.4 million. January is lowest. It has the highest spending per tourist, but so few tourists that its total is still the smallest.

stem: Total spending by tourists in May was approximately what percent greater than in March?
explanation: May: 50,000 × 480 = 24.0 million dollars; March: 30,000 × 550 = 16.5 million. The increase is 7.5/16.5 ≈ 45%. The trap 67% is the increase in the number of tourists alone (20/30), ignoring that each tourist spent less in May.

stem: What was the total spending by tourists in June, in millions of dollars?
explanation: June had 45 thousand tourists spending an average of 520 dollars each: 45,000 × 520 = 23,400,000 dollars, or 23.4 million.

text: Average hours per week that students in four age groups spend on homework, reading for pleasure and screen time

stem: By what percent is the average weekly homework time of the 16-17 group greater than that of the 10-11 group?
explanation: Homework rises from 5 to 14 hours, an increase of 9 hours. As a percent of the 10-11 base, 9/5 = 1.8 = 180%. The trap 280% is 14/5, the 16-17 figure as a percent of the 10-11 figure rather than the increase.

stem: For the 12-13 group, approximately what percent of the total time spent on the three activities is screen time?
explanation: The 12-13 group spends 7 + 5 + 16 = 28 hours on the three activities, of which 16 are screen time: 16/28 ≈ 57%. The option 43% is the share of homework and reading together (12/28).

stem: Indicate all age groups for which average weekly reading time is less than half of average weekly homework time.
explanation: Half of homework time is 2.5, 3.5, 5 and 7 hours for the four groups. Reading time (6, 5, 4, 4) is below half only for ages 14-15 (4 < 5) and 16-17 (4 < 7). For the two younger groups, students read more than half as long as they do homework.

text: Tickets sold and ticket prices for five shows at a city theater during one season

stem: Which show earned the second-highest ticket revenue (tickets sold × price per ticket)?
explanation: Revenue for each show: Drama 310 × 30 = 9,300; Musical 580 × 45 = 26,100; Opera 150 × 60 = 9,000; Dance 240 × 40 = 9,600; Comedy 420 × 25 = 10,500 dollars. Comedy is second after the Musical. Opera has the highest price, but it sold so few tickets that it earned the least.

stem: The Musical's ticket revenue was approximately what percent of the total ticket revenue for the five shows?
explanation: Total revenue is 9,300 + 26,100 + 9,000 + 9,600 + 10,500 = 64,500 dollars, and 26,100/64,500 ≈ 40.5%, about 40%. The trap 34% is the Musical's share of tickets sold (580/1,700), which ignores the different prices.

stem: How many more dollars of ticket revenue did Comedy earn than Drama?
explanation: Comedy earned 420 × 25 = 10,500 dollars and Drama earned 310 × 30 = 9,300 dollars, a difference of 1,200 dollars. Comparing tickets sold alone (110 more for Comedy) leaves out the prices.

text: Exports and imports of goods for Country V, 2021-2025

stem: For which year was the ratio of exports to imports the greatest?
explanation: Exports exceed imports only in 2023 (61/57 ≈ 1.07) and 2025 (66/60 = 1.10); in the other years the ratio is below 1. So 2025 has the greatest ratio. Watching only the gap between the bars is risky: 2023's and 2025's gaps (4 and 6 billion) are close, so compute the ratios.

stem: From 2021 to 2025, the percent increase in exports was approximately how many percentage points greater than the percent increase in imports?
explanation: Exports grew from 48 to 66 billion: 18/48 = 37.5%. Imports grew from 55 to 60 billion: 5/55 ≈ 9.1%. The difference is 37.5 − 9.1 ≈ 28 percentage points. The option 18 is the increase in exports in billions of dollars, and 38 is the export growth rate alone.

stem: Indicate all years in which exports increased by more than 10 percent over the previous year.
explanation: Compare each year with the one before: 2022 rose 4/48 ≈ 8.3%, 2023 rose 9/52 ≈ 17.3%, 2024 fell, and 2025 rose 8/58 ≈ 13.8%. The rises in 2022 (4 billion) and 2025 (8 billion) look modest on the chart, but only 2022's is under 10% of its base.

text: Intended major areas of the 2,400 students in a university's first-year class, and the percent of each group who are international students
table: International students (percent of the major area)

chart.title: First-year class by intended major area (2,400 students)

stem: Of the international students in the first-year class, approximately what percent intend to major in Engineering?
explanation: Count international students in each area: Engineering 40% of 720 = 288, Business 30% of 600 = 180, Sciences 25% of 480 = 120, Humanities 10% of 360 = 36, Arts 20% of 240 = 48, for 672 in all. Engineering's share is 288/672 ≈ 42.9%, about 43%. The trap 40% is the table entry, which is the share of Engineering students who are international, not the share of international students who are in Engineering.

stem: Which major area has the greatest number of first-year students who are not international students?
explanation: Domestic students = students × (100% − international %): Engineering 720 × 0.60 = 432, Business 600 × 0.70 = 420, Sciences 480 × 0.75 = 360, Humanities 360 × 0.90 = 324, Arts 240 × 0.80 = 192. Engineering leads narrowly. Business is the trap: it has a higher domestic percent than Engineering, but on a smaller group.

stem: What percent of the entire first-year class are international students? Give your answer to the nearest whole percent.
explanation: There are 288 + 180 + 120 + 36 + 48 = 672 international students out of 2,400: 672/2,400 = 0.28 = 28%. Simply averaging the five table percentages gives (40 + 30 + 25 + 10 + 20)/5 = 25%, which ignores that the groups differ in size; the overall rate is a weighted average.
